column1: # title: ENG-205 Canterbury Analysis — 4 Main Ideas

column2: Because male clerks' books limit remarriage and sex, the Wife opens by treating lived "experience" as more reliable than bookish "auctoritee," then cites scripture only when it serves that claim.
Five marriages, climaxing in Jankin's nightly antifeminist book and the blow that deafens her, teach her that without maistry over tongue, body, house and land she stays under male rule.
Once Jankin burns the book and gives her the bridle and all the sovereinetee, they have "never debate," and she is as kind and true to him as any wife, so yielded mastery produces peace.
The knight's quest proves women want sovereignty and maistrye; when he yields "wise governaunce," the old wife chooses to be both fair and good, and they live in parfit joy.
Unlike blunt estates satire, Chaucer's narrator suppresses overt blame and even admires dubious skills, so readers must draw the ironic criticism out of details offered as praise.

Phrases such as "countrefete cheere of court," "I said his opinion was good," and "the beste beggar in his house" sound admiring on the surface while the same words mark vanity, a monk out of cloister, or corrupt skill.
